bib.title: Consensus is Strategically Insufficient: Reasoning-Trace Disagreement as a Knowledge-Representation Signal

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Consensus is Strategically Insufficient: Reasoning-Trace Disagreement as a Knowledge-Representation Signal", Michał Wawer and Jarosław A. Chudziak (Warsaw University of Technology), arXiv:2606.04223v1 [cs.AI], 2 Jun 2026. Preprint (AAAI-style format, no venue stated).

COVERAGE: 24465 of 24465 chars read (all pages, including references). No appendices exist. Nothing skipped. Figures not extracted (I used the text only).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: This is a position paper with a small check, not a benchmark. Its core argument is that majority vote, debate and consensus all treat disagreement as a defect, and that this is insufficient for value-laden tasks where disagreement can be a stable property of the case.
  number: none
  setup: Argued for content moderation (KEEP/REMOVE). The authors say the framework "is normative".
  quote: "We argue that this objective is insufficient for value-laden tasks, where disagreement may reflect genuine normative uncertainty rather than agent error."
  where: Abstract, p.1

- Claim: Four disagreement states come from two axes. One axis is mean pairwise similarity of reasoning traces against threshold θs. The other is the top-decision share p* against threshold θa. Each state has a default routing rule: CA -> Auto, DA -> AutoExplain, DD -> SeekContext, CD -> Escalate to a human.
  number: 4 states, 4 meta-actions
  setup: n agents each output a reasoning trace, a binary decision, a value profile and a confidence. Both thresholds are "a policy parameter, not a universal semantic boundary".
  quote: "R1 :CA(c)⇒Auto(c, d ∗)... R2 :DA(c)⇒AutoExplain(c, d ∗)... R3 :DD(c)⇒SeekContext(c)... R4 :CD(c)⇒Escalate(c)."
  where: Sec. 3, p.2

- Claim: Convergent disagreement (similar reasoning, split decisions) is the key state. It is read as a different weighting of values on a shared description of the case, so forcing consensus there may hide a normative conflict. Divergent disagreement is read as ambiguity, which calls for more context instead of human review.
  number: none
  setup: Interpretive claim, not tested causally.
  quote: "forcing consensus (Denisov-Blanch et al. 2025) here may conceal rather than resolve a normative conflict."
  where: Sec. 3, p.2

- Claim: The rules are defeasible, so domain rules can override the state-based defaults.
  number: none
  setup: Hand-designed rules.
  quote: "HighRisk(c)⇒Escalate(c), LegalRequirement(c)⇒Escalate(c), and LowRisk(c)∧HighEscCost(c)⇒AutoExplain(c, d ∗)."
  where: Sec. 3, p.2

- Claim: The states track human annotator disagreement in the predicted order DA < CA < DD < CD. The pooled gap between the two disagreement states and the two agreement states has Cohen's d = 0.80.
  number: d = 0.80, p < 1e-11, n = 600. Mean human disagreement: DA 0.351 (n=118), CA 0.638 (n=24), DD 0.751 (n=382), CD 0.782 (n=76).
  setup: Five agents from one base model, differentiated only by system prompts (harm-focused, context-sensitive, community-norms, free-expression, legal-framework). Data is the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, 600 items stratified by human annotator disagreement. Similarity is cosine similarity of embedded traces. The base model is not named in the text.
  quote: "The two disagreement states {CD, DD} are jointly separated from the two agreement states {CA, DA} with effect size Cohen's d = 0.80 (p <10 −11, n = 600)"
  where: Sec. 5, Table 1, p.3
  note: DD holds 382 of 600 cases (64%) and CA only 24, so the states are very unevenly populated. The CD vs DD difference (0.782 vs 0.751) is small, and no test is reported for it. CA (0.638) sits well above DA (0.351), which the paper does not explain.

- Claim: Category-based flagging beats a divergence-only baseline (1 - mean similarity) at predicting high human disagreement, but only modestly.
  number: F1 0.548 vs 0.503 vs random 0.401. Precision 0.401 / 0.347 / 0.333. Recall 0.845 / 0.915 / 0.505.
  setup: Same 600 items. Both methods use the same operating point.
  quote: "Category-based escalation 0.401 0.845 0.548 / Divergence only 0.347 0.915 0.503 / Random baseline 0.333 0.505 0.401"
  where: Table 2, p.3
  note: The authors say the F1 numbers are not what carries the argument: "The result we treat as load-bearing is qualitative the ordering and the agreement/disagreement gap, rather than the specific F1 numbers." Precision of 0.401 is barely above the 0.333 random baseline.

- Claim: Multi-agent debate, round-table consensus and Byzantine-tolerant aggregation share one design assumption: that disagreement is transient and must be resolved before output.
  number: none
  setup: Related-work framing.
  quote: "share a design assumption that dis-agreement is a transient state to be resolved before output."
  where: Sec. 6, p.3

LIMITS
- Authors concede these limits:
  - "Prompt-based perspective differentiation may underrepresent the heterogeneity of independent agents."
  - "Embedding similarity is a coarse proxy for reasoning equivalence."
  - The routing rules are "hand-designed defaults rather than learned or formally verified policies."
  - The check covers a single domain and a single corpus.
  - They call it "a sanity check on the KR layer, not a benchmark of the routing policy."
- What it does not show (my reading):
  - It never runs the routing policy end to end.
  - It does not compare outcomes against majority vote or debate.
  - It has no correlated-error measurement.
  - Human disagreement is the only ground truth.
  - It does not report which LLM was used.
  - The thresholds θs and θa are not reported.
  - No error bars are given beyond one p-value.
  - Its claim that CD signals normative pluralism is untested, because the check only shows that human disagreement is higher.
- Scope: the claim applies to value-laden tasks only. The paper says plainly that consensus is plausible for instrumental or factual tasks. It is not evidence against majority vote on factual tasks.
- Agents are clones of one base model with different prompts. So the paper does not address correlated errors across identical-model agents, even though the setup invites that question.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Du et al. 2024, multiagent debate (ICML).
- Liang et al. 2024, divergent thinking via debate (EMNLP).
- Chen, Saha and Bansal 2024, ReConcile (ACL).
- Zheng et al. 2025, Byzantine fault tolerance view of multi-agent systems (arXiv preprint).
- Zhang et al. 2025, multi-LLM-agent debate scaling (ICLR 2025 blogpost track).
- Wang et al. 2025, Mixture-of-Agents (ICLR).
- Denisov-Blanch et al. 2025, "Consensus is not verification: Why crowd wisdom strategies fail for LLM truthfulness" (arXiv:2603.06612). This is the paper cited for the consensus-failure point.
- Wawer and Chudziak 2026, "When AI agents disagree like humans" (ICLR 2026 HCAIR workshop). This is the direct predecessor and supplies the experimental setup.
- Kennedy et al. 2020 and Sachdeva et al. 2022 (Measuring Hate Speech corpus, perspectivist NLP).
- Dung 1995 (argumentation), Brewka, Dix and Konolige 1997 (nonmonotonic reasoning), Grossi and Pigozzi 2014 (judgment aggregation), List and Pettit 2002, Austen-Smith and Banks 1996 (Condorcet jury theorem).

CODE: none. The only formalism is the four rules above (Sec. 3, p.2) and the state definitions: CA = HighSim ∧ Agree, DA = LowSim ∧ Agree, CD = HighSim ∧ Disagree, DD = LowSim ∧ Disagree (Sec. 2, p.2).

FIGURES (text only; not extracted with the figures script)
- Fig. 1 (p.2): a 2x2 grid of reasoning similarity against conclusion agreement, with a default meta-action in each cell (CA Auto, DA AutoExplain, DD SeekContext, CD Escalate). This is the best single figure candidate. It conveys the whole taxonomy and routing table at a glance. Caption: "The four disagreement states arise from combining reasoning similarity with conclusion agreement. Each state has a default meta-action σR (Sec. 3). Convergent disagreement is treated as the strongest candidate signal of value-laden conflict."
- Fig. 2 (p.3) is the controller architecture. Fig. 3 (p.3) is a bar chart of mean human disagreement per state.

FIT TO TARGET NOTES
- For 05-topology-patterns.md (aggregation design): it is a useful counterpoint. The aggregator can be a router on the disagreement structure instead of a vote. Cite it as a design proposal with preliminary evidence, not as a measured gain.
- For 07-failure-modes-at-scale.md (correlated errors): it is weak support. It does not measure correlated errors and does not test factual tasks. The nearest relevant point is the Denisov-Blanch citation, which I did not read.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean apart from some mangled table layouts and equations. Table 1 columns are parsed in order (State, Description, n, Mean). Figure 3 is a bar chart whose text shows values only. No embedded instructions were found in the PDF text.
